title: Autoimmune neutropenia in children & adolescents – diagnostic approach, longtime course and psychosocial impact
summary:
Neutropenia is defined as a reduced number of neutrophils in the blood. Neutrophils are a subgroup of white blood cells and play an important role in defending against bacterial infections. Patients with too few neutrophils may therefore be more susceptible to bacterial infections. There are various causes of neutropenia. So-called autoimmune neutropenia occurs particularly in infants and children. In this condition, the body produces autoantibodies (proteins which, for example, also help to confer protection following vaccination) against the neutrophils, causing them to be broken down at an increased rate and resulting in a reduced number of neutrophils in the blood. The condition is usually self-limiting (it resolves without treatment); nevertheless, the course of the disease varies considerably among affected patients.
Very little is known about the factors relevant to the development of neutropenia and its subsequent course, for example in terms of susceptibility to infection and the need for treatment. 
Furthermore, it is not known to what extent this chronic condition affects the families of the young patients.
The aim is to investigate the extent to which the course of the disease differs or, conversely, is similar amongst those affected. Various aspects of their medical history will be compared. The impact of this chronic condition on family life will also be examined.

interventions.name: Data will be gathered by studying available paper-based documentation like doctor’s letters, medical reports and lab reports. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Informed consent
Diagnosis of AIN
at least one follow-up visit in our Department of Pediatric Hematology and Oncology
Diagnosis of reactive neutropenia, severe congenital neutropenia, alloimmune neutropenia, cyclic neutropenia
Exclusion criteria:
Absence of informed consent
Neutropenia due to treatment of malignant disease
